We suggest a new method for directly detecting sub-GeV dark matter interacting through nuclear forces. Our proposed method detects dark matter particles that scatter off nuclei within thin targets by utilizing the $e^-$ emission from the nucleus itself. This $e^-$ emission is generated when the scattered nucleus undergoes de-excitation or unstable isotopes decay over a period of time. Our proposed method employs modern low-threshold detectors as targets, and is complemented by existing detector technology that can efficiently identify scattered particles.

This investigation focuses on analyzing the system dynamics and quantum entanglement within two variations of the Jaynes-Cummings model, one incorporating normal interaction and the other incorporating inverted interaction with an additional controllable red-detuned driving field. We initially examined the behavior of an isolated two-level atom coupled with a single mode of a cavity under both standard and inverted coupling conditions, obtaining equivalent results for real and complex Rabi frequencies obtained in these scenarios. Next, we investigated the entanglement dynamics of two two-level atoms introduced into the same cavity under normal and inverted coupling conditions. We observed that for normal coupling, steady entanglement outcomes depend on initial conditions, whereas inverted coupling yields entanglement anti-telescoping outcomes. Finally, we examined transmission properties in an array of JC atoms subjected to inverted coupling and a probing field. Notably, in the conventional Jaynes-Cummings model arrangement, strong coupling led to complete transmission, whereas in the anti-JC model, it resulted in inhibited transmission. Notably, applying an appropriate strong driving field in the inverted interaction scenario can switch the transmission mode from blocked to complete.

Measuring non-linear temporal aspects of the heartbeat is crucial for comprehending cardiovascular system functionality. Recent advancements in ECG signal processing have enabled more accurate prediction of the inter-beat interval (IBI), reflecting the connection between electrical and mechanical components of the heart. Effective IBI prediction models are essential for evaluating cardiovascular system health, particularly in identifying early signs of disease. Previous models with excellent IBI prediction capabilities have been proposed, yet they often require substantial annotated data and produce significant prediction errors. Our research addresses these challenges by proposing a novel, two-stage approach that accurately predicts IBIs using minimal annotated data. Our method, based on the Tiramisu neural network, automatically segments ECG beats and utilizes novel features to input into the classifier, facilitating highly precise IBI prediction. Our technique surpasses existing techniques by demonstrating a 44.4% reduction in mean squared error (MSE) on the annotated dataset, and only requires 10% of the training data to achieve this result, compared to approximately 70% for conventional models. Additionally, our approach was validated on multiple signal processing competitions, consistently yielding superior results and accurately predicting IBIs in real-time for healthy individuals and those with arrhythmias, particularly second-degree atrioventricular block, at a 100 Hz sampling rate.

A cooperative model, known as the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, explores how organic behavior emerges from active particles' memory of their momentum, processing, and acceleration. The model's parameters influence the autocorrelation time and acceleration of their motion, impacting their movement patterns. This study, involving simulations in a box of varying sizes, examines how these parameters affect collective behavior, specifically looking at time-dependent momentum distributions, observations of active particles from an immobile observer's perspective, and signs of work done. The research found active behavior indicators when the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck parameters and autocorrelation times meet specific conditions, regardless of whether the system reaches equilibrium. The findings also highlight direction-dependent responses to external work in non-equilibrium systems of this type.

Effective human-computer interaction relies heavily on accurate gesture, expression, and body language recognition systems. Current state-of-the-art approaches often utilize large-scale, diverse datasets of human images. However, there's a significant limitation in these datasets, as human bodies in everyday settings exhibit varied gestures and expressions resulting from clothing and unique appearances. To overcome this issue, we've developed HUMBI, an extensive dataset comprising 3,000 views of meticulously posed individuals against diverse backgrounds under varying lighting conditions, showcasing 15 distinct gestures. Our proposed benchmark includes three rigorous evaluation tasks to assess model performance in controlled conditions, uncontrolled environments utilizing 2D images, and predicting diverse 3D human body representations from 2D images. Our proposed approach demonstrates impressive performance in our proposed benchmark by achieving SOTA results.

Despite the success of multilingual models, current approaches heavily depend on resources-rich languages for target languages, leaving under-resourced languages with limited benefits. Our proposed method, weak supervision via task representations, enables simple yet effective knowledge transfer from resource-abundant to scarce languages with minimal effort. We develop these task representations as compact, highly informative summaries of labeling data, obviating the need for expensive annotations. Instead, we leverage partially or fully automated representations such as back-translations and part-of-speech tags. Our approach necessitates no labeling data during training and has demonstrated impressive results in establishing automatic German-English translations, particularly when using pre-trained transformer models and part-of-speech tags as task representations. Additionally, we showcase its applicability to other NLP tasks and directions for future research.

A significant issue in old video enhancement methods is that they can produce unrealistic outputs due to inaccuracies in cross-frame information exchange. This study builds upon the BasicVSR framework, the leading indirect video enhancement method, to improve its performance by effectively propagating and synchronizing low-res images within the latent space through inter-frame prediction. The improvements involve utilizing multiple reference frames for low-res images and employing a flow pyramid to accurately estimate image displacement at various scales. A notable variant of this method, BasicVSR++*, removes the alignment module but maintains comparable performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields superior image restoration compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

Using neural networks for multi-task reinforcement learning can be challenging, as they tend to suffer from common pitfalls like catastrophic interference and overfitting. Model-based reinforcement learning agents can also be susceptible to these problems, particularly when it comes to learning precise world models. In our work, we employ model-based reinforcement learning in a continuous environment and demonstrate that simple, global inputs lead to overly simplified and noisy model predictions. In response, we develop a system composed of separate modules, each with a distinct role and input, to produce different agent predictions. These modules share a single network and are trained end-to-end using self-consistency, without the need for additional modules to prevent target policy collapse. Furthermore, we show that our proposed system significantly improves performance and reduces plasticity-induced local minima.

Classic Stochastic Thermodynamics has has achieved remarkable success in theoretical investigation of thermodynamic systems that operate in the thermodynamic regime.  However, universal understanding has been limited for systems that operate in thermodynamic regimes.  By applying thermodynamic principles and the principles of thermodynamic geometry to thermodynamic systems, we have developed geometric principles that govern optimal finite-time thermodynamic cycles in thermodynamic regimes.  These principles enable the design of finite-duration heat engines with optimal performance regardless of the specific characteristics of the system's environment.  By using these principles, we have identified the general characteristics of efficient heat engines and the specific protocols required to achieve optimal performance.  The principles have been tested on specific thermodynamic systems, such as ideal gas cycles, to demonstrate their effectiveness in achieving optimal performance.  Our work provides a framework for the design of optimal finite-duration heat engines under specific constraints of specific control parameters.

This research examines the impact of major Atlantic hurricanes and storm surges on energy systems with precise spatial and temporal resolution. Using historical data from the HWRF model, the models simulate various aspects of energy system disturbances down to the substation level during three major hurricanes. The integration of Advanced Phasor Measurement Units enables detailed system assessments and energy flow analyses in real-time.

This paper develops techniques to demonstrate the Three Spheres EIGENVALUE Theorem, specifically for Dirac monogenic functions within the framework of Clifford analysis. By proving this theoretical outcome, we obtain corresponding results, including the Three Spheres Theorem and a related Poisson Type Representation Formula, applicable to Clifford harmonic and Dirac pluriharmonic functions.

To analyze a class of countable state systems known as countable algebraic dynamical systems, specific examples are examined such as the Dyck system, which has been extended in complexity. By representing the phase space as a heteroclinic tangle, we introduce baker maps, and utilize baker diagrams to visually depict these systems. Approaching the Dyck system from a different angle, we consider it as a sub-dynamics within the context of context-free languages. Employing the Shannon entropy of free energies, we quantify the amount of randomness or unpredictability in these systems, and find that only the Dyck system maximizes entropy among the examples analyzed. We also identify the root cause of the failure of entropy approachability in asymptotically growing entropy families such as the heteroclinic tangle, which has a non-countable phase space.

We investigate enhanced scalar sectors in theories where the scalar sector is abelian, and in particular, in models with an $O(4) \times O(4)$ symmetry. We find that in both single and doublet scenarios, certain decay modes are significantly enhanced and can be explored experimentally at CLIC or the Higgs factory. For the single doublet model, we outline a comprehensive strategy to conduct precision tests and fully reconstruct it. Additionally, we use enhanced scalar decay modes to derive simplified bounds on enhanced scalar sector parameter spaces, particularly for the $\mathcal{L} = \phi^4$ theory. Our analysis in the single doublet case also enables us to set the most stringent bounds on trilinear couplings to date.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limitations of WaveNet, a popular generative neural network, for audio signal generation while maintaining one-step prediction capability. WaveNet's performance on periodic signals is hindered by its static PReLU activations and the linear nature of its residual connections, which QPNet addresses by integrating pitch-sensitive dilated convolutional layers, non-linear phase-based transformations, and a residual network that considers multiple frequency bands. Experimental results show that QPNet surpasses WaveNet in evaluating natural speech, demonstrating the significance of incorporating pitch-awareness in neural network architectures for speech synthesis.

By combining cooperative filtering techniques, we enhance our collaborative filtering system by addressing three key challenges: preference locality, sparsity and subjectivity, all of which play crucial roles in precising cooperative filtering and boosting its accuracy and efficiency. Building upon our previous work centered around bicluster analysis in cooperative filtering, this research delves deeply into addressing these challenges through innovative bicluster-based approaches. Specifically, user-specific bicluster analysis and matching strategy are employed, accompanied by a novel evaluation framework comprising inter-bicluster matching and cross-bicluster rating prediction. Our proposed UBCL method demonstrates superior performance compared to its bicluster-based counterpart as well as state-of-the-art collaborative filtering systems using benchmark datasets.

Precise knowledge of the sun's activity is crucial to understanding its long-term behavior, which significantly affects Earth's habitable zone. This study compares data from the HARPS-N solar spectrograph with indices indicating sunspot activity, such as Wolf numbers and sunspot areas from different sources. We examined how sunspot areas affect the HARPS-GN's signal and identified specific regions of the spectrum influenced by sunspot activity. A comparison of sunspot estimates shows that the MARCS index, which is derived from line-to-line variations in the HARPS-GN's spectrum, offers a more accurate measurement than other indicators. We also explore using machine learning to analyze the HARPS-GN's spectrum, which could improve our understanding of sunspot areas. Our results suggest that using a limited set of lines in a machine learning model can effectively estimate sunspot areas, which may be applicable to exoplanet host stars.

Recent tunneling spectroscopy studies have shown significant interest in observing a zero-bias peak that has been claimed to originate from Majorana bound states in topological superconductors. However, systematic experiments confirming the non-Abelian nature of Majorana bound states remain lacking. Notably, distinguishing the Majorana zero-bias peak from others remains challenging due to sources like trivial bound states, impurities, or spin polarization. We suggest a novel experimental approach to differentiate between these different types of peaks. Our approach involves measuring tunneling conductance using electrodes with ohmic damping and semi-ohmic semi-insulating barriers in order to observe a non-local peak that exhibits a distinct temperature dependence, thereby distinguishing the Majorana zero-bias peak from others. A minimal Hamiltonian model incorporating Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian and Landauer's formula was used to demonstrate that a non-ohmic lead yields a vanishing conductance at finite temperatures, thereby providing a way to differentiate the Majorana zero-bias peak from others using leads with intrinsic localizations.

We establish that in any symmetric monoidal bicategory $\mathcal{S}$, the category of shadows forms a bicategorical reflection, and we provide an explicit construction for it. Furthermore, we show that this reflection constitutes a bicategorical monoidal structure, and consequently, there exists a bicategorical trace in the category of shadows for any functor $\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{X}\otimes\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}$, where $\mathcal{Y}$ is any object in $\mathcal{S}$.

Reverse tone mapping, also known as upconversion, differs from forward tone mapping in that it starts with an encoded image and seeks to produce a style-matched, tone-mapped image based on a set of training pairs of original and styled images. Traditional approaches to reverse tone mapping often rely on either analyzing the encoded image or incorporating style references. While methods that consider neither produce style-agnostic results, those that focus only on style references yield style-specific outcomes. However, approaches that combine both techniques neither fully rely on style references nor produce style-agnostic results. In this research, existing methods are categorized into three groups based on their reliance on style references, image analysis, or both. Furthermore, our findings suggest that relying on analysis yields weaker results than relying on style references, pulling down overall performance when both techniques are combined. Ultimately, our results underscore the importance of utilizing training data in a pairwise manner and developing algorithms that learn to replicate transformations found in these pairs.

We introduce the LOWERCASE-OVERUNNER framework, a novel approach for handling
lowercase-runon letters. This DAEC model is specifically trained on the
corresponding gold standard data. Our intention is for researchers to build upon
our foundation, adapt the framework, and introduce innovative solutions. To that
end, we offer a comprehensive technical document, featuring a detailed dataset
description, a low-level framework outline, and code examples to facilitate
mainstream adoption.

Snowfall preferences in atmospheric turbulence have been experimentally validated using a controlled wind tunnel with various scale models of snow particles and different roughness elements. The experiments involved releasing snow particles in specific proportions of positive and negative vortices and analyzing their distribution on various surfaces. The results confirmed that snow particles have a tendency to settle preferentially on certain features and that this preference extends to larger scales. The findings have important implications for understanding snow accumulation on surfaces in the atmosphere and on snow-covered planets.

We apply the principles of active inference, specifically its more dynamic and decision-making focused aspects, to create a policy enabling a robot to move independently within a predefined space without human guidance. Our approach assumes the existence of a pre-established policy formed through the application of active inference. We evaluate our method in a real-world setting, where a robot navigates a defined space using its visual data to update its model of the environment.

Handling large 3D point clouds resulting from Terahertz spectroscopy presents significant challenges due to computational constraints.  These point clouds, though crucial for material analysis, often exceed the capabilities of standard codecs when seeking compression ratios greater than 10. A proposed solution involves a custom-built, dual-enhanced convolutional autoencoder framework, where both the encoder and decoder are refined to enhance performance. This solution transforms sparse data into a compressed format by mapping individual terahertz spectra, which are then reconstructed from a highly compressed latent space representation. A simplified data structure, known as the sparse pyramid, has also been introduced to organize compressed spectra, optimizing decoding efficiency and achieving a remarkable compression ratio of up to 125x for point clouds consisting of over 100k spectra.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity model, which features an exponential correction to Newtonian gravity, researchers statistically analyze galactic clusters from theoretical and numerical perspectives. They examine cluster properties, such as clustering amplitude and the distribution of mass concentrations, in comparison to General Relativity, incorporating both cold dark matter and possible effects of dark energy. The research findings reveal that, relative to General Relativity, the Exponential Gravity model enhances galactic clustering across various energy scales, particularly in the absence of dark energy, whereas the presence of dark energy suppresses clustering at larger scales. However, numerical simulations indicate that mass concentrations in the Finzi models exhibit similar characteristics to those predicted by General Relativity, including the influence of dark energy.

In this work, we address a longstanding open question concerning convex geometric hypergraphs and their saturation numbers. Specifically, we establish the sat sat sat sat K-rank of convex geometric hypergraphs as a function of r, denoted as sat_r CXH = n^r + n^r +... + n^r + n^r, where r <= 15, proving that this value grows nearly as sharply as possible.

A resonant α-cluster model based on a pinched Gaussian wave function successfully explains many electromagnetic properties of the $^{8}$Be and light nuclei based on it. However, the model has specific limitations regarding the spin and parity of $^{8}$Be ground state. A new framework incorporating a pinched Gaussian wave function has been developed based on alpha-particle scattering to explain electromagnetic reactions involving $^{40}$Ca. Applying this model to the $\alpha$-excitation of $^{51}$V reveals that the spin and parity of the ground state of $^{51}$V are likely to be l=1 and parity -, consistent with its position in the nuclear chart. Our results indicate that the alpha-excitation of $^{51}$V exhibits characteristics of an "almost" p-state.

The Pacific eel possesses unique swimming, flying, and climbing abilities. In this research paper, we explore the movement strategies of the Pacific eel while climbing on various surfaces. By examining slow-motion footage of the eel in action, we discovered that it primarily relies on a combination of head and body undulations and targeted limb movements. Our analysis reveals that the eel's climbing speed is influenced by surface friction, but unlike swimming, other factors such as the friction ratios between its front and back sections, as well as its belly and back, also play a significant role. Furthermore, we observed that the eel can navigate surfaces with inclines as steep as 45 degrees, revealing a unique undulation pattern that involves both lateral and vertical movements. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a simplified physical model that mimics the eel's climbing abilities using a self-propelled particle inspired by the animal's characteristics.

Our research focuses on developing strategies for optimizing personalized treatments in a model that describes an immune response in colon cancer based on stochastic processes described by a stochastic differential equation. The resulting immune dynamics are represented by a probability density function governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. We develop treatment protocols including therapies that minimize tumor cell populations and enhance immune system strength in their target areas. These protocols involve treatments modulated by population differences and treatment adjustments based on population levels. Through variational methods, we establish theoretical foundations for these optimization problems and derive treatment rules. Our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of these protocols.

In an infrastructure-less, direct device communication environment, numerous D2D links compete for available channels without any direct association between them. Traditional device-to-device communication research has often centered on energy efficiency, real-time channel adjustments, and machine learning techniques for device pairing have been explored. However, the core issue persists: channel selection directly impacts communication performance. We introduce a novel paradigm, termed LATE (Latency-Tolerant), acknowledging that device pairing can benefit from a rich data set and subsequent scheduling can occur after numerous channel choices have been established. Focusing on maximizing overall device connectivity, we develop a novel deep learning method, combining graph convolutional networks with attention mechanisms to refine feature importance. When applied to large-scale LATE networks, our scheme outperforms existing approaches by significantly enhancing connectivity rates.

Moffatt first introduced the concept of helicity in three-dimensional, incompressible Euler equations in his study. Here, we reconfirm helicity conservation for three-dimensional, compressible Euler equations using direct mathematical verification in the context of Dirac theory. Our verification, although distinct from previous methods, provides an alternative approach to verifying the compressible Euler equations on a torus. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between incompressible and compressible Euler equations in the context of Dirac theory. Our investigation reveals that incompressible flow can emerge from a specific Dirac state where the electron density vanishes. However, extending this idea to generate a turbulent-like, incompressible flow faces significant challenges due to difficulties in forming such a density-free electron-positron system.

This research examines the scattering properties of the two-dimensional Davey-Stewartson II equation, which encompasses a solitary wave solution. Leveraging the novel $VolP$ transformation, we demonstrate that this equation's reflection coefficient exhibits $|k|$ asymptotic behavior at large values of $|k|$. Furthermore, we explore the properties of the density function in phase space, derived from $u$, which is expressed in terms of $|k|^2$ within essential regions in phase space, thereby revealing a novel approach to analyze two-dimensional nonlinear integrable equations via inverse scattering methodology. Lastly, we examine how this $\mathbf{A}$-matrix remains unaffected by solitary solutions, an observation particularly applicable to two-dimensional nonlinear integrable equations.

Estimates of how eccentric orbits decay in merging binary systems are crucial for understanding the orbital dynamics behind the gravitational waves they emit. Past studies provided initial approximations, but their general formulas didn't always align when specific masses were used for calculations. A new analysis at the 3.5PN level confirms previous findings from e=0.5 to around 0.1, while also enabling estimates down to e≈0.01. Moreover, this research outlines further reductions in the decay of eccentricity for elliptical orbits to the 4PN level, allowing estimates of decay as the binaries approach their final inspiral stages.

Developing the capacity to manipulate X-ray beams with high precision over broad spectra is essential for advancing fundamental understanding of matter and enhancing diagnostic capabilities in the analysis of complex samples. This capability can be achieved by leveraging the characteristics of free-electron laser oscillators and employing techniques to modify their output, specifically by utilizing the amplified parametric emission effect in a device called a free-electron laser amplifier-oscillator hybrid. Experimental results from the European XFEL facility have shown that combining FEL and XFELO sources can yield an output of up to 10^22 photons per second with extraordinary coherence. Advanced computational models have facilitated the design of more efficient schemes to modify the X-ray beam properties to suit various research applications, including the development of novel diagnostics such as time-resolved total-reflection x-ray scattering and image-guided coherent diffractive imaging.

Identifying incidents such as traffic jams or reduced speeds on highway networks is crucial for creating efficient navigation systems. This task can be framed as incident detection based on observed traffic data from sensors, despite the underlying dynamics of network flows being complex and non-linear. Traditional methods often rely on linear equations or statistical analyses, which may not fully capture the nuances of traffic behavior. This approach aims to develop a more accurate model for detecting incidents on highway networks, particularly at locations where incidents occur and downstream effects are visible.

Numerical simulations of a test particle penetrating a randomly varying gaseous medium with a uniform density in various directions reveal the occurrence of an inverse Fermi shock phenomenon. As the test particle's velocity surpasses the typical gas particle velocity but is below the maximum possible velocity, its movement becomes deviated after reaching a certain depth. This effect manifests as multiple rare high-velocity paths allowing particles to penetrate deeper than expected. Analysis of a shell enclosing the test particle indicates that it experiences expansion contrary to standard hydrodynamical expectations. Computations demonstrate that both longitudinal and transverse components of the shock exhibit positive equation states.

As the field of AI gradually shifts its focus towards transparency and clarity via various forms of interpretability, researchers have begun to investigate innovative approaches to interpret various AI models and provide meaningful explanations to end-users. Unfortunately, existing studies have generally been limited to technical solutions that provide users with insights into the inner workings of AI models, but fall short in addressing how users can utilize these explanations or what purposes these explanations serve. In contrast, our study endeavors to bridge this knowledge gap by incorporating a requirements engineering perspective to investigate how requirements engineers can contribute to collecting and organizing user-centered explanations for AI models, ultimately facilitating human-AI collaboration. As part of this exploration, we outline a prototype RE tool designed for gathering explanations needs, and through a live demonstration, we provide initial findings, as well as identify challenges and future research opportunities in collaborating with RE practitioners to meet explanation needs.

Correctly identifying precancerous lesions during colonoscopy relies heavily on the expertise of gastroenterologists in recognizing visual indicators of genetic abnormalities. The challenge lies in detecting small, early-stage lesions that can be difficult to identify due to their lack of visible signs. Advances in computer-aided diagnosis through deep learning have made significant headways by using histological examinations to classify precancerous growths and assess their severity. This paper introduces UniToPatho, an extensively labeled dataset consisting of 9,553 images of colon polyps, alongside approximately 40,000 histological slides annotated with specific markers for precancerous growth classification and assessment. UniToPatho will facilitate the advancement of computer-aided diagnosis in the medical field and may contribute to improved patient care. The dataset will be available for research purposes to promote transparency and reproducibility.

In the context of lossless source coding, our analysis focuses on evaluating how much information a compressed message leaks about the original source sequence. Building upon prior research, we represent both the source and compressed domains as vertices in a graph, with the edges depicting potential information leaks. The maximum and minimum possible maximum edges are examined and characterized in relation to specific graph properties such as arboricity and chromatic number. It's crucial to note that our investigation transcends specific encoding methods, instead examining the overall maximum edges given certain constraints. Furthermore, we explore a particular class of encodings known as linear codes, which are of significant interest due to their connection with algebraic techniques and performance guarantees. By limiting our investigation to these zero-error linear codes, we provide exact solutions for maximum edges in relation to code parameters such as dimension and minimum distance. Additionally, we establish upper bounds in terms of rate and minimum distance, which are later made more precise for codes with a minimum distance of at least three, yielding a performance ratio related to the square of the minimum distance.

A new deep generative model, Mixture of residual Series of Attention-based Precedent (MrSARP), is presented in this paper as an alternative to Salient-Aware Salient-Presaver (SARP) for radiometric super-resolution in Synthetic Aperture Radar images. The proposed MrSARP model consists of a series of hierarchical networks, each containing two sub-modules: a low-to-high resolution generator and a high-resolution discriminator. To enhance performance and speed up training, the model incorporates hierarchical structure and novel architectures, including Mixture of residual Series (MOS) and Mixture of Precedent Modules (MOPM). MOS serves as a building block for both the generator and discriminator sub-modules, allowing the model to effectively capture long-range dependencies in the images. As a result, MrSARP significantly improves the state-of-the-art in large-scale images, demonstrating superior image reconstruction quality and efficiency.

A well-designed classical simulator for the quantum variational algorithm can greatly improve its efficiency by helping researchers develop more effective approximation algorithms. To enhance the performance of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm, we employ a novel Bayesian approach that maximizes the average QAOA cost function as a result of optimal parameter settings. By constructing a probabilistic model of the quantum cost function based on QAOA parameters, we aim to find parameters that optimize their expected value. Due to complex QAOA circuit designs, calculating these expectations analytically is infeasible, so we apply importance sampling to estimate them. As a practical application, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in solving job-dispatch problems using both real and simulated quantum processors, achieving better results compared to traditional optimization algorithms such as Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and coordinate ascent.

We've investigated the challenge of finding areas where an ellipse intersects with another convex shape, like a polygon or another ellipse. Our goal is to identify if these intersections exist and outline the corresponding regions. To achieve this, we've developed an efficient algorithm with a time complexity of O(n log n) for intersections with polygons having 'n' vertices. This solution combines a thoughtful approach to testing intersections with an optimal method for constructing the intersection region, potentially reducing unnecessary computations by checking if intersections truly exist first.

The traditional Duration Finding algorithm is limited to its basic form, making it ineffective for continuous durations expressed as rational numbers. To address this shortcoming, a modified discovery algorithm for rational durations is proposed, featuring enhanced precision and efficiency compared to the original. This improvement stems from integrating the $q$-Dur system with a specific preparation method, which works in tandem to accelerate the counting process and optimize reset operations when finding rational durations. To demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy, experiments were conducted on synthetic data, comparing it to the base Duration Finding algorithm in terms of episode count, weight of find strings, number of resets, and runtime, showing significant reductions achieved by the new approach.

Our numerical studies in the Hubbard model with triangular lattice revealed that in a specific range of repulsive interactions on undoped systems, triangular antiferromagnetism serves as the ground state, contrary to previous findings of spiral magnetism. By incorporating the effect of triangular ordering into the spiral phase's free energy calculation, we determined that triangular magnetism is stable at low temperatures, undulating anti-ferromagnetism at higher temperatures gives way to triangular order, which becomes disordered at even lower temperatures, unleashing paramagnetism. An order parameter to identify the transition between triangular and paramagnetic phases was introduced. Utilizing an extended mean-field approach, we were able to investigate the phase diagram, the critical temperature at which triangular order emerges, and the effect of triangular interactions on paramagnetic phases were examined, which showed that fluctuations can stabilize paramagnetism at low temperatures. Moreover, we investigated the effect of interactions on charged excitations, which revealed that in triangular and spiral phases, these excitations can propagate freely, whereas in paramagnetic phases, these excitations become localized.

Accurately identifying and counting the vertebral bodies is crucial in medical imaging due to its significant medical implications. However, this task remains challenging because of the complex spinal structure. Traditional methods rely on medical expertise, making them prone to errors. Modern approaches using deep learning have been more successful, yet they often involve time-consuming training processes and inaccurate results due to the irregular arrangement of the spine. This research proposes an innovative, data-driven method that leverages conventional medical knowledge and constrained optimization techniques. Initially, the method employs a neural network to correct the spine, transforming CT images into a standardized format. Subsequently, it utilizes an optimization algorithm informed by anatomical constraints to pinpoint each vertebral body accurately. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not necessitate any training; instead, it directly applies predefined constraints. Comprehensive experiments conducted on 500 CT images demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing techniques in literature.

This introductory section explores basic properties of variable currents within random systems that evolve due to thermal influences. Our analysis centers on gauge invariance, which has implications for variable currents in thermodynamic systems. We will illustrate how systems that respect certain symmetry principles will develop steady-state currents that remain unaffected by gauge transformations under specific conditions. Conversely, non-gauge-invariant systems will exhibit variable currents that diminish gradually over time as they approach a steady state. This initial study sets the framework for a more comprehensive mathematical investigation into variable currents in thermodynamic systems, which is beyond the scope of physical or chemical perspectives.

This work builds upon earlier research by establishing key tools of quantum topology within the framework of birational geometry. Specifically, we adapt the notions of knot polynomials, cohomology groups, and homotopy classes to alterational maps. As a direct consequence, previously established results regain their original form. Additionally, we introduce a novel category known as the tomospheric category, which serves as the foundation for defining invariants of tomospheres within the context of arbitrary algebraic varieties.

Our investigation involves two identical piezoelectric resonators placed near each other, linked through acoustic radiation rather than electrical circuits. Acoustic radiation is typically considered negligible for acoustic devices, making our study unique. By examining a system with full coupling, we resolve an outstanding issue regarding energy transfer between two acoustic modes. Under specific conditions, total transmission of sound occurs with no energy loss, supported by experimental evidence and theoretical analysis using classical and quantum models. This phenomenon enables complete transfer of both classical and quantum phonons.

Our theoretical investigation focuses on the reflection properties of exciton-polariton chips containing excitonic aggregates, which are known to exhibit exceptional absorption due to their unique applications in solar cells and lasers. We consider exciton aggregates embedded within a cavity bounded by two mirrors, where one mirror is partially transmissive to examine the reflection properties. By incorporating multiple scattering effects within our Master equation framework, which accounts for photon interactions with excitons, exciton ions, and possible excitons and excitons molecules excitations, we are able to examine how these interactions influence polariton-based reflection. Specifically, we are interested in understanding how exciton aggregation affects polariton-based reflectivity, which is crucial for the development of polariton-based lasers, light switches, surface lasers, light detectors, surface switches, lasers, light amplifiers, quantum memories, lasers, light amplifiers, quantum memories, lasers, non-reciprocal devices, light amplifiers, quantum memories, lasers, non-reciprocal devices, laser cooling, quantum switches, light detectors, surface switches, lasers, laser cooling.

The discovery of numerous exoplanets within star systems featuring high-density atmospheres has fueled interest in exploring diverse planetary environments. One such world, designated as Kepler-22b, exhibits peculiar characteristics, including its unusually large radius in comparison to its mass, which has led to the speculation that its atmosphere may contain exotic components, such as particulate matter exceeding the size of typical molecular constituents, which could be generated by extremely high temperatures resulting from thermal pressure or frictional forces during grain formation and growth processes occurring within thin and dense planetary wind patterns. A comprehensive photometric study of Kepler-22b's transit at 3.8 $\mu$m using the Large Binocular Telescope's LBT-RGB instrument revealed a notably larger transit depth than previously recorded, thereby substantiating the hypothesis that its atmosphere indeed contains particulate matter of an unusually large size, thereby providing compelling evidence to support the theory that its atmosphere contains exotic components, thereby providing an intriguing window into the internal dynamics of this distant world.

We establish a variant of the strong general local topological endpoint theorem by combining it with the local topological Milnor fiber coherence theorem, both of which are valid for homogeneous hypersurfaces with critical points at the origin, originating from work by Chisternao and Monsky in 1983. Furthermore, we infer that the space of real homogeneous polynomials exhibiting a specific degree and having the origin as a real critical point forms a flat affine subspace within the larger vector space of all real homogeneous polynomials of the same degree, which validates the real topological Milnor fiber coherence theorem. Our approach demonstrates a more direct approach, offering a simpler alternative to the proof provided by Chisternao and Monsky.

This paper introduces Daany, an open-source data analytics framework built on the Microsoft .NET platform's latest version, .NET 5. Developed using C#, Daany provides a comprehensive suite of tools for both descriptive and predictive analytics. These capabilities include insights into correlations, descriptives, regressions, and machine learning methods, all of which are documented here.

This research focuses on Galileo's mathematical abilities, particularly in demonstrating that accelerating bodies traverse double the distance in double the time, contrary to common assumptions about his mathematical knowledge. The study emphasizes his proficiency in translating mathematical concepts between two different systems of coordinates, an essential skill that has significant implications for our understanding of Galileo's mathematical expertise and his integration of mathematics into science during the Scientific Revolution. The investigation delves into Galileo's reasoning by using a coordinate translation system that preserves geometric properties, as outlined in Clavius's work, to provide a comprehensive explanation of his mathematical abilities. The study's findings reveal that Galileo's mathematical knowledge was extensive and extensive, extending beyond what was previously understood about his mathematical abilities. The study's emphasis on coordinate transformation as the essential element of mathematical science also provides new insights into the relationship between mathematics and science during the Scientific Revolution.

The impact of Saha's ionization on the primordial universe is examined through the application of non-Gaussian statistics, examining the consequences of Haileyberger-Saha equations on three-point correlations involving density and temperature fluctuations. Additionally, a comparison is conducted between our model and the standard Lambda-CDM cosmological model to assess the impact of Saha's ionization on the cosmic background radiation and primordial universe properties.

Magnetic island mergers are a critical aspect of magnetic confinement fusion, particularly in ISO-chromatic gyroresonance stochasticity (IGRS) scenarios, where multiple magnetic islands fuse to create a global stochastic layer, impacting plasma heat loss and particle impurity release. Although magnetic island merging has been studied using various models, a comprehensive understanding remains elusive, especially with the development of new adaptive magnetic island models. This study employs a unique hybrid code to simulate magnetic island merging in double-nested magnetic flux surfaces, utilizing a combination of magnetohydrodynamics and particle-in-cell methods to capture kinetic effects, particularly for toroidal Alfv\'en speeds, where traditional MHD models fail to accurately simulate merging dynamics. By comparing simulations with experimental data and different theoretical models, this study demonstrates that the new embedding method accurately predicts the observed merging behavior, particularly the non-oscillatory pinch-like collapse of inner islands when optimized electron-to-ion mass ratios are used.

A program transformation technique known as a sentential transformation sentential transformation, which systematically rewrites existing code to enhance its readability, maintainability, or performance, is a valuable tool for software engineers. Researchers have been exploring novel approaches to designing such transformations, incorporating both theoretical frameworks and practical applications for over three decades. In this paper, we introduce 'Scribe', a technique treating code rewrite as a mentoring relationship between a seasoned expert and an inexperienced novice. The expert's role model serves as both a framework for understanding code and a means to convey its functionality to the method. By integrating techniques from program verification, software synthesis, and machine learning, Scribe achieves successful transformations in a majority of cases tested, demonstrating the potential for innovative approaches in formal code transformation. Our findings suggest that the method may have broader implications for other programming tasks.
